newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to pursue close relations with Latin America.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to pursue close relations with Latin America.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Friday the United States would pursue close relations with Latin America, but expressed concern about current political turmoil in Ecuador.

Albright made her comments after talks with Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria in a meeting she said symbolised the importance of the United States' friendship with its Latin American neighbours.

Albright said in a press conference the United States was "watching very closely" the events in Ecuador, where on Thursday the Congress voted President Abdala Bucaram out of office on grounds of mental incompetence. Bucaram, known as "El Loco," has vowed to resist efforts to oust him.

"We want to make absolutely sure democratic practices are carried out there," Albright said. "We have been so very proud of the tide of democracy in this hemisphere, so the carrying out of democratic practices is very important."

Albright said her meeting with Gurria here at Rice University was her first with a foreign official outside of Washington since taking office last month and, as such, should be seen "as a sign of the importance and richness of our relationship."
She noted that President Bill Clinton would be making his first trip to Latin America in April.

"We have a golden opportunity to develop the strongest relations in the Americas," Albright said. "We are in a new phase of dealing with democratic governments that are developing economically in a most satisfactory way."

But she had harsh words for Cuban leader Fidel Castro, whom she described as "dinosaur" who represents "a system that does not work." She also pledged her support of the Helms-Burton law, which restricts trade to Cuba and has been criticised by many U.S. allies, including Mexico.
The two said their talks touched on topics ranging from immigration to human rights to the Chemical Weapons Conventon.

Albright said the two had agreed to deal with immigration issues in a "legal and sensitive manner." Regarding the often-criticised human rights situation in Mexico, she told reporters: "I explained that we are following the law of the land, that human rights is a signature element of our foreign policy."

Gurria praised the Clinton administration for its current campaign to convince the U.S. Congress to join the Chemical Weapons Convention, a global ban that takes effect on April 29 but has not been signed by the United States.
"We're satisfied that this effort is being put on by the administration. We think it's a very critical issue," he said. Mexico already has signed the weapons ban.

Albright, in response to a reporter's question, also spoke about recent revelations that members of her family had been Jews who were killed by Nazis during the Second World War. Albright's parents raised her as a Catholic in the United States.
The disclosures, she said, had tempered what she described as the "happiest time" of her life.
"Great moments of happiness are also accompanied by great moments of sadness, and clearly this is a very bittersweet time for me," she said.
